mechanism: Higher flow sweeps away Mo-S species faster, raising local supersaturation and nucleation density (nonlinear at very high flow).
Moving transversely into faster flow/lower precursor residence reduces Mo supply per site, giving smaller domains.
Low flow gives insufficient transport while high flow dilutes/removes precursor, so domain size peaks at intermediate flow.
Coverage peaks at intermediate Ar flow where MoO3 delivery is optimal; too high flow starves or blows away precursors.
More MoO3 raises Mo vapor supersaturation, producing multilayer/thicker growth rather than monolayer.
Insufficient S leaves suboptimal sulfurization, while excess S suppresses MoO3 reduction/transport; domain size peaks at intermediate S.
Higher temperature boosts precursor flux and adatom diffusion, increasing coverage and eventually thicker multilayers.
Small gap gives high local Mo concentration and multilayers/nonuniformity, large gap gives sparse growth; best uniform monolayer at intermediate gap.
Higher MoO3 temperature raises vapor flux and supersaturation, increasing nucleation density and thereby reducing/altering grain size.
Higher substrate temperature lowers supersaturation and raises desorption, reducing nucleation density while enlarging domains via diffusion.
Changing S/Mo ratio shifts flake morphology from truncated/irregular shapes to triangles and alters size via edge-growth kinetics.
Thinner MoO3 film supplies less Mo, lowering nucleation and growth so crystals are smaller.
Higher temperature depletes the thin MoO3 faster and lowers supersaturation/raises desorption, reducing coverage density.
More MoO3 nanoribbons provide more local Mo source, increasing coverage.
